1:
When the psalm was written is disputed, and the answers sort the voices. Adam Clarke holds it composed during the Babylonish captivity and says plainly that David could not be its author; the title must apply to an Asaph who lived under the captivity, or to the family, or to a band of singers still bearing that name. Some think Jeremiah composed it, since the sixth and seventh verses are exactly those of Jeremiah 10:25. John Calvin agrees and rejects the alternative outright: those who ascribe it to David allege that the afflictions were predicted by the spirit of prophecy, but it is not usual with the prophets thus to speak historically in their prophecies. He puts it either when the Assyrians had burnt the temple, or when Antiochus defiled it. Keil and Delitzsch call the psalm the pendant of an earlier one: both have the same Asaphic stamp, both stand in the same relation to Jeremiah, and both complain out of circumstances only the age of the Seleucidae and the Chaldaean period can exhibit. Charles Ellicott leans the same way, observing that the third verse is freely quoted at 1 Maccabees 7, introduced by the phrase according to the word which he wrote, as though a contemporary were meant.

Augustine of Hippo takes the opposite line and keeps the psalm with David. When these things were sung in the times of King David, he points out, nothing of the sort had befallen Jerusalem by the hostility of the Gentiles, nor the temple of God, which was not then even built — for it was after David’s death that Solomon made a temple. That is therefore spoken of as past which in the Spirit was seen to be future.

What was violated they set out in order. John Gill takes the inheritance for the land of Canaan, out of which the heathen had been cast to make room for Israel, and which is called the Lord’s because he dwelt in it; or the city he chose to put his name in, or the temple itself, which it was always a profanation for a heathen to enter. Charles Ellicott thinks the word probably intended to embrace both land and people, and glosses heaps as ruins. C.H. Spurgeon hears a cry of amazement at sacrilegious intrusion: the stranger pollutes the hallowed courts with his tread and forces his way into the inmost sanctuary, so that holy land, holy house and holy city were all polluted by the uncircumcised. It is sad to see the foe in our own house, he adds, but worse to meet him in the house of God — for they strike hardest who smite at our religion.

Matthew Henry draws the same order of grief into a rule. Canaan was dearer to the pious Israelite as God’s inheritance than as his own; injuries done to religion should grieve us more than those done to our own right, so that we should better bear to see our own inheritance wasted than God’s.

The unburied dead draw the closest notice. Adam Clarke says the Chaldeans would not bury the slain but left them to birds and beasts of prey, which he calls the grossest inhumanity, and that the Jews not slain were carried captive, so none remained to do it. John Gill observes that good men who served the Lord suffered in the common calamity, at the captivity and under Antiochus. Charles Ellicott notes that the word for saints alludes to a party named in 1 Maccabees, and that the scenes still witnessed at the Jews’ wailing-place illustrate these verses, showing how deep-seated the love of an ancient place is in the Oriental mind. Adam Clarke names the neighbours who gloried in the subjugation — Idumeans, Philistines, Ammonites and Moabites — and says their insults were mixed with blasphemies against God.
5:
The question opening this section is heard as the note of an age. Charles Ellicott calls how long, Lord the dominant cry of that age. John Gill explains why it is asked: what was done was done by the enemies of the Lord’s people, yet by his permission and as a token of his anger against them — hence the expostulation. Adam Clarke puts it in one sentence: wilt thou continue thine anger against us, and suffer us to be insulted and thyself blasphemed? C.H. Spurgeon presses the jealousy. There was great cause for it, since idols had been set up and Israel had gone aside from his worship; but the psalmist begs him not to consume his people utterly as with fire, but to abate their woes.

The petition that follows is an imprecation, and the voices are careful about it. John Gill grants the form but denies the motive: these words, though in the form of an imprecation, regard not private revenge but public justice and the honour of God. They may also be considered a prophecy of God pouring out the vials of his wrath on the antichristian states, who though they profess Christianity are no other than heathens. Matthew Henry makes the same move: the prayer is in effect a prophecy, in which the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. Adam Clarke argues from comparative guilt: bad as we are, we are less wicked than they, for we have been unfaithful, but they never knew thy name and are wholly abandoned to idolatry.

C.H. Spurgeon makes the appeal more openly and admits what it rests on. If thou must smite, he has the psalmist say, look further afield: there are lands where thou art in no measure acknowledged, so visit these first and let thine erring Israel have a respite. Hear us the prayerful, and avenge thyself upon the prayerless. Then he names the difficulty squarely: sometimes providence appears to deal much more severely with the righteous than with the wicked, and this verse is a bold appeal founded upon that appearance.

Who the heathen are Matthew Henry settles from the second clause. The reason men do not call upon God is that they do not know him, how able and willing he is to help; and those who persist in ignorance of God and neglect of prayer are the ungodly, who live without God in the world. There are kingdoms that know not God and obey not the gospel, he says, but neither their multitude nor their force will secure them from his just judgments. Of their crime he is brief: they have devoured Jacob, and that is crime enough in the account of him who reckons that those who touch his people touch the apple of his eye. They have not only encroached upon his dwelling place but laid it waste; and the prayer asks not merely that they be restrained from further mischief but that they be reckoned with for the mischief already done.

The last clause draws a note on the word and one on the authorship. Charles Ellicott renders dwelling place literally as pasture, a figure he says is a favourite in the Asaphic group of psalms. Adam Clarke reports that the Chaldee understands it of the temple, which was by eminence Jacob’s place, and returns to his earlier point that these two verses are almost identical with the passage in Jeremiah, which has led many to think Jeremiah the author. C.H. Spurgeon keeps to the image: the oppressor would quite eat up the saints if he could, and if these lions do not swallow us it is because the Lord has shut the lions’ mouths. John Gill extends the devouring to the church of God, made havoc of by the Romish antichrist, and the laying waste to Jerusalem and the temple.
8:
What the former iniquities are John Gill canvasses at length. The Greek gives our ancient iniquities, and the most ancient sin of all is that of our first parents, from which flows the corruption of our nature. Or the phrase may mean the sins of our youth, as Kimchi takes it, or the sins of our fathers, as Aben Ezra, which the Lord sometimes visits upon the children. Some think the reference is to the golden calf, and Gill reports the Jewish saying that no punishment happens to Israel but there is an ounce in it for the sin of the calf. Adam Clarke keeps to the shortest of these: visit us not for the sins of our forefathers.

Whether the psalmist admits any guilt of his own generation is the question Charles Ellicott raises and answers cautiously. How, he asks, is the petition to purge away our sins to be taken in connection with the verse before it? Does the psalmist admit guilt in his own generation as well as in those of former times, or is he thinking only of the inherited guilt and punishment? The general tone of the post-exile psalms, he says, inclines towards the latter view. Of the verb itself he notes that it means rather to put a cover on, and compares the way Cicero speaks of political crimes being covered by the plea of friendship. Adam Clarke renders the same verb be propitiated, or receive an atonement on account of our sins.

The prayer that mercy would prevent them is read as a race against ruin. Adam Clarke takes it of mercies going before, to turn us out of the path of destruction, and renders the next clause literally — we are greatly thinned, few of us remain. John Wesley compresses the whole petition into three words: prevent our utter extirpation. John Gill sets out what the help asked for amounts to: to be brought out of their troubles, to be enabled to bear them without murmuring while God pleases to continue them, and to be given more grace in time of need. The arguments enforcing the petition, he adds, are that God is the God of salvation, of whom alone it is to be expected, and that to help and save is for the glory of his name.

The taunt of the heathen closes the section. John Gill says nothing can be more distressing to the Lord’s people than to be asked where the God is whom they boast of and put their confidence in, as though he had forsaken them and would not help. Adam Clarke turns the taunt into the petition itself: show where thou art by rising up for our redemption and inflicting deserved punishment upon our enemies. Charles Ellicott traces the form of the question to Joel and would render the next clause let it be known — that is, let it be known where God is, let the answer to the question be given in vengeance, and let us see it.
11:
Who the prisoners are they agree about, and about the darker phrase they differ. John Gill takes them for prisoners in a literal or spiritual sense, whose sighs and groans are not hid from the Lord but come up into his ears as did those of the children of Israel in Egypt. John Wesley names them simply as God’s poor people now in captivity, and Charles Ellicott notes that both this expression and the one following occur at Psalm 102:20 of the sufferers in the Captivity. Adam Clarke takes the second phrase literally as sons of death, and allows it two senses which he applies to the same people at once: those condemned to death for their crimes, and those condemned to be destroyed by their oppressors — the Israelites being both.

The sevenfold recompense is where the chapter’s ethics come into view. John Gill guards the measure: not sevenfold for one, as the Targum paraphrases it, nor a sevenfold punishment for a single sin, but that God would recompense their sins largely and abundantly, though not beyond measure or exceeding the rules of justice. Adam Clarke keeps it concrete and reciprocal — let them get in this world what they deserve for the cruelties they have inflicted on us, and let them suffer in captivity who now have us in bondage — adding that this is probably a prediction rather than a wish. Charles Ellicott declines to soften it and states the difficulty instead. The measure is the sevenfold of Genesis 4:15, he says, and we naturally contrast the law of Christian forgiveness. He explains the figure of the bosom from dress, the deep folds of the Eastern garment being used as a pocket, and observes that the sharpest pang of the suffering came from the taunts of neighbours.

The closing verse is read as the answer to everything that preceded it. John Gill distinguishes the title: they were God’s people not by creation and providence only, as all men are, but by special choice and covenant grace; and the sheep of his pasture are those he feeds as a shepherd feeds his flock. Adam Clarke makes the same points more briefly and turns the verse into the last petition — let us not be destroyed by those who are thy enemies, and we in all our generations will give thanks unto thee for ever.

C.H. Spurgeon takes the gratitude as lasting as it is deep: on the church’s tablets are memorials of great deliverances, and as long as she exists her sons will rehearse them with delight, since we have a history that will survive all other records. From the direst calamities God’s glory springs, he adds, and the dark days of his people become the prelude to unusual displays of the Lord’s love and power. Charles Ellicott closes with a remark of Burgess on the last word of the psalm, praise: the one crowning privilege of God’s people, the exulting and triumphant confidence in God which only his chosen can entertain and express, placed here in splendid contrast with the reproach of the heathen and of the malicious neighbours of the verse before — let them curse, so long as thou dost bless.
